_about: Identification key for /holding — 'I'm holding an amulet'. The reader answers the sian's first questions (เนื้อ material, then what the eye sees) by tapping; the page answers with candidate KINDS. Class facts (resident / upkeep / provenance_sensitivity) are read at build time from wichaa-vault/_meta/vocab/classes.md and are NOT duplicated here. The figures×materials mapping below is this page's own curation (src says whose claim each kind is: 'vocab' = the kind is a member term in the vault class vocabulary; 'curated' = added here, with class left null where the vocabulary does not place it). Market counts come from catalog.db at build time via the search terms, with the delete-then-test excludes rule from axis_match (a page holding both a real hit and a stray collision still counts).

brass, bronze, copper, silver — cast or struck, with a coin's shine or a statue's weight

excludes: องค์สมเด็จ
kinds.what: A rectangular pressed tablet of sacred powder bearing a seated Buddha in an arch — the most copied, most collected amulet form there is. Power is the maker's barami and the consecration; nobody is home.
A small cast Buddha with a pellet sealed inside — shake it and it chimes. Cast in bronze or nawaloha in the Chinese-Tibetan medicine-Buddha line.
A figure with hands over its eyes — the shut-away senses. Pressed powder or cast metal; worked for warding and for wealth that slips past notice.

kinds.term: เหรียญพระเกจิ
search: เหรียญหลวง
เหรียญรุ่น
kinds.what: A struck coin-form medallion carrying a revered monk's portrait, name and temple, usually dated to the batch (รุ่น). The most datable of all forms — the coin itself says when.
A small cast statue of a monk seated in meditation — the medallion's three-dimensional cousin, from pendant size up to the altar.

An amulet recovered from a sealed temple cache (กรุ) — fired earth or chin alloy more often than powder, with the crust and mineral bloom of centuries in the chamber. Age is the whole question; the surface is the testimony.
A monk's photograph sealed under glass or resin, often with powder, hair, or robe-cloth packed behind the image — a portable reliquary in costume jewellery's clothes.

A sheet of metal — or palm-leaf, or skin — inscribed with a yantra and rolled tight, worn on a cord at the waist or neck. Power lives in the inscription and the rite that closed it. The treatises this site keeps are full of what gets written inside.
A cloth square or banner drawn with grids, figures and script — hung over a door, folded into a pocket, or worn. The drawn designs have their own index here: /yant.

A cowrie shell loaded with sealed mercury and bound in cord or foil — the classic 'undoer' that turns aside harm and bad medicine. The formulary in this corpus carries a making ascribed to Luang Pu Bun of Wat Klang Bang Kaew.

A knife forged and inscribed as an instrument of the doctor-of-spirits — for cutting what binds, not what bleeds. Manuscript 6983 in this corpus records a ten-iron forge recipe from Wat Pradu Song Tham.

kinds.fuzzy: The vault vocabulary deliberately does not assign this a class: an impersonal luck-and-commerce charm to some keepers, a guardian-spirit vessel to others. It needs a knower, and the page says so rather than deciding.
kinds.what: A carved or cast phallic rod, pocket-carried for luck, trade and protection — one of the oldest charm forms in the region, and one the tradition itself files two different ways.

kinds.fuzzy: The sharpest seam in the whole register, measured not decreed: Buddha-amulet FORM, but many makings carry prai-kuman MATERIAL. Its upkeep is an amulet's; its provenance question is a spirit-object's. Ask what went into the batch.
kinds.what: A pressed tablet in the classic arch — named for the epic's charm-master, and the one amulet whose material story matters as much as its form. Some are pure powder; some are worked with necromantic material, and the difference does not show on the surface.

kinds.term: พระผงใบลาน
kinds.what: Pressed from the ash of burnt palm-leaf manuscripts — the same leaves this archive catalogues, at a later moment of their life. A treatise here gives the recipe outright: inscribe five leaves with katha, burn, mix with lacquer, roll.

A child figure that is not a depiction but a home: a bound child-spirit, raised as family — fed sweet red drink and rice, named, spoken to, asked for help. The corpus holds the historical making in full, framed as ethnography, at manuscript 6983.

kinds.fuzzy: Raised like a kuman, made from untimely death like a prai — the vocabulary places it with prai as the more careful reading, and marks the line splittable by a knower.
kinds.what: A small preserved or effigy foetus-form, kept in oil or cloth — kuman-adjacent in the raising, prai-adjacent in the origin. Of all the kinds on this page, the one whose history most deserves asking in full.

A figure of cloth, wax, wood or metal, animated by yantra and spell to serve and guard — a compelled animation rather than a named ghost. Manuscript 6983 gives two makings, and this site keeps a working companion at /hun.

kinds.term: น้ำมันพราย
search: น้ำมันพราย
kinds.what: An oil rendered by rite from a ghost of violent or untimely death, sold in vials and worked mostly for compulsion in love and trade. The tier the tradition itself cautions hardest about: fed, and closed properly when set down.
A female ghost of untimely death housed in a figure or locket — the classic แม่นางพราย of the caution-tales. Keeping is a knower's work in the vocabulary's plain words: feeding, and correct closing.

kinds.fuzzy: Class depends entirely on the making — some waxes are herbal and impersonal, some are prai-worked. The pot does not say; the maker's lineage does.
kinds.what: A wax or balm in a small tin, touched to lips or brow before speaking, selling, courting. The corpus's formulary holds attraction-wax recipes; what a given pot is depends on whose hands made it.
A plant of power — a rhizome or tuber grown, dried, carved or potted, its virtue in the species and the keeping. The one kind on this page that can still be alive; some keepers water theirs.

kinds.term: ท้าวเวสสุวรรณ
kinds.what: The northern guardian-king of the yaksha, club in hand — statue, pendant and gate-plaque. A deva venerated through the object: offerings and respect, not meals.
The king of birds, wings spread — authority, safe passage, and debt that dares not follow. Cast in metal from pendant to standard.
Rahu swallowing the moon, classically carved into a one-eyed coconut shell — the astrological remedy worn by those in a Rahu period. This site's almanac pages keep the sky half of the story.
The shop-keeper's lady, hand raised in the customer-calling gesture — shelf statue and pendant both. Venerated with respect and small offerings; every market in the country works under her hand.

kinds.term: รูปพระฤๅษี
kinds.fuzzy: The class vocabulary does not yet carry the lersi as a member term; most keepers treat the figure as a teacher venerated on wai-khru days rather than a resident to feed. Carried here ahead of its vocabulary entry.
kinds.what: The tiger-skinned hermit sage — the tradition's own teacher-figure, honoured at every wai khru. A treatise in this corpus gives a moulding recipe: termite-mound earth and seven named leaves, shaped into the Great Lersi.

kinds.gloss: the temple boy of Wat Chedi
kinds.fuzzy: The largest new devotion of the era and not yet in the class vocabulary. Kept mostly as a votive relationship — ask, promise, and deliver what you promised — rather than as a fed dependent; a knower may file it more precisely.
kinds.what: The boy-spirit of Wat Chedi in Sichon, the biggest devotional wave since Jatukham — asked for lottery luck and repaid in firecrackers and toy soldiers. The amulet carries the devotion; the vow-keeping is the keeping.

kinds.gloss: the beggar who never left empty-handed
kinds.fuzzy: Not in the class vocabulary; kept by traders as an asking-figure — venerated, not fed — and filed here ahead of a knower's ruling.
kinds.what: The jataka's tireless beggar, carried by sellers and askers on the logic that no one ever refused him. A statue-and-pendant devotion of the marketplace.

kinds.term: พญาเต่าเรือน
kinds.what: The house-turtle amulet in the line of Luang Pu Liu — slow money that stays, long life, a household that holds. Blessed object, no resident.

kinds.term: เขี้ยวเสือ
search: เขี้ยวเสือ
kinds.what: A fang — tiger classically — carved or capped in metal, its power in the animal's own authority. Natural talisman: nothing conferred, nothing to feed. Modern pieces are mostly carved substitutes, which the honest seller says.

A dark lustrous metal the tradition holds to be alive — drawn from caves by rite, said to drink honey and turn aside blades. Power inherent in the thing itself; the category every faker loves, which is its own caution.

kinds.term: กะลาตาเดียว
search: กะลาตาเดียว
kinds.what: A coconut shell with a single eye where every normal shell has three — a natural anomaly, not a crafted thing, carved (often into Rahu) or kept whole. The rarity IS the charm.
A stone-hard concretion found grown inside a coconut — one of the คด family of impossible stones found in living things. Kept whole as found; power inherent, none to feed.

The paired myna birds of sweet speech — carried by sellers, suitors and anyone who must be believed. Usually a small couple of birds in metal or wood, or the yantra of them; the yant index here draws the design.
The arahant who never lacked — staff over shoulder, umbrella and kettle — carried for provision that arrives on time. Statue and pendant, venerated as an ordinary amulet.

A quid of betel a revered monk himself chewed, dried and kept — a bodily relic in the most literal sense, priced accordingly in the living market. Power is the master's barami; keeping is plain respect.
